title: Portfolio CMS
description: I built a local Express content management system that compiles this entire site into a single 300KB file, not including the media.
longDescription:
Existing website builders always lock away some layout tweak or charge monthly fees to host a basic portfolio. My old workflow meant cutting videos in ClipAmp and hosting them on YouTube, which left content fragmented across external platforms and slow to load. I wanted everything in 1 place, running locally, with 0 recurring costs.

I built an administrative panel using vanilla JavaScript and an Express server that runs on my laptop. Dropping a video or photo into the editor triggers an automated pipeline that strips video audio, encodes to 1080p H.264, converts images to WebP, and sorts them into project folders. The front end runs React 18 from a CDN and reads from a JSON block. Updating a project now feels as fast as moving desktop files around, though I am still fixing an offset bug that leaves a black gap on mobile screens.

When I hit publish, the server merges the media and JSON data into index.html in under 10 seconds. That build process keeps the final footprint under 300KB. Pushing the project directory to GitHub Pages updates the live site immediately.

title: Immersive Dance Lighting Rig
description: We packed two hundred moving lights into the room, but running them at full brightness emptied the dance floor.
longDescription:
The physical ceiling forced a massive life-safety detour before we even hung a light. We were building a dense hybrid rig for the main room at Temple San Francisco, centering on a curved video ceiling that wrapped down behind the DJ. Because the solid ceiling plane blocked standard fire suppression, I brought in a crew to reroute the sprinklers above and below it using side sprayers with a 15-foot reach. When we found the main sewer drain blocked, we had to cut in a new basement drain just to clear the system. We hung a strut channel grid from scissor lifts, leaning heavily on a laser level to line up the video panels down the center of the room. Nearly 200 moving lights flanked the screens.

My goal was the rig had to vanish into the dark when unlit. We built ten custom pillars out of OSB and drywall mud, sinking aluminum LED extrusions into the corners. We also salvaged chipped acrylic and old LED strips lost in the building to build 32 VIP pixel tables. Because pandemic PPP loans covered wages instead of materials, it made sense to have my skeleton crew build them by hand. I wired the entire rig onto switched relays grouped in fours, so fixtures wouldn't sit sucking dust on dark days.

The real fight was the software backend. I wanted video content to carry over into the pixels and the lighting rig, but the lighting console couldn't switch back to independent color control fast enough. I rebuilt the routing from the ground up several times. The trick was using Madrix as the central processing hub. I fed ArtNet data from Resolume and a Roadhog 4 console into Madrix on unused universes, merged them, and pushed that out to the decoders. Getting the room to act as one system took weeks. My go-to test was a single diagonal line sweep. I would slow it down to see how closely the systems aligned as the line dragged across the ceiling, down the back wall, and across a double-sided video monolith sitting in the middle of the dance floor.

The owner wanted every fixture and screen blasted at 100 percent all the time. I argued that crowding that many lights into a small room is about angles and combinations, not raw brightness. When we opened, they tested that full-blast look on the crowd. Within ten minutes, people left and the dance floor was almost entirely empty.

title: Emmy Stand
description: I lit the gold statue with miniature boom towers, locking the current limit so the plastic wouldn't melt.
longDescription:
An old coworker from my club days won an Emmy. He asked for a custom display, so I scaled ballet lighting principles down to a desktop rig. The stand uses three boom towers per side that arch from downstage to upstage, plus angled wall washers recessed along the outer edges. A dual-material film strip lines the bottom for diffusion and masking.

The curved backdrop was too large for a single print. I built it in modular sections and turned the seams into an exaggerated surface texture. When I set the statue on the pedestal, the gold finish mirrored the light sources instead of absorbing them. The metal warped the reflections.

Packing 512 LEDs into closed plastic is basically building a slow toaster. To keep the enclosure from melting from the inside out, the hard fabrication rule was power management. I locked the current limit to three amps before I ever turned it on.

title: LithoLab
description: A client-side web application that generates multi-color lithophanes in custom shapes with an exportable border for 3D printing.
longDescription:
Four-color generators output rectangular prints and turn skin tones into magenta splotches. I wanted multi-color prints in custom shapes with an independent border, so I ported the PIXEStl engine to run client-side in a browser. Hosting the application on GitHub Pages kept it lightweight without server overhead.

Running mesh processing locally hit strict cache limits in the browser immediately. Early prints on a Bambu Lab X1C also exposed a persistent micro-gap along the right edge between the lithophane and its border, which took several of failed attempts to eliminate. I stripped the calibration tools out of the main application and built LithoPalletGen as a standalone utility to keep the primary interface clean. This companion app handles color mapping for any filament palette, extending past 4 colors to fix the banding on faces.

My own printer runs an 8 color setup across 2 AMS2 units, but the software supports any palette size. Once calibrated and backlit, the physical prints match the source photos.

gallery.caption: The LithoLab workspace links source image manipulation directly to physical 3D print parameters. In the main canvas, users apply custom geometric masks and adjust spatial orientation, while the sidebar controls physical dimensions, border scaling, and filament palette selection. The dual-preview engine at the bottom provides immediate feedback, displaying both a palette-accurate color rendering and a surface-texture depth map to verify print accuracy before exporting.

title: Unfold
description: A browser-based card game with 4 prompt decks, built with local save states for video calls.
longDescription:
Unfold started as a quick prototype on Lovable to generate conversation cards for video calls. The game runs 4 prompt decks across 3 play modes to move discussions past routine small talk. Since the app needed no user registration or backend databases, paying for a subscription platform made no sense. I pulled the codebase into a dedicated GitHub repository and hosted it statically on GitHub Pages.

To avoid server costs, I used Cursor to build a local save-state layer using React Hooks and browser storage. That setup tracks previously seen cards and stores custom decks directly on the client. Built with Tailwind CSS and Radix UI primitives, the interface handles deck combining and card draws without dropping state.

title: Pyramid
description: I trapped a pixel matrix inside a sealed 3D print and accidentally mushed the melting plastic with my thumb.
longDescription:
I wanted a pixel effect on the surface of a 3D object. To get it, I built a glowing pyramid with a subdivided grid inside.

Getting crisp isolation without light bleed meant printing the sculpture as a single piece. Every layer needed a black core to block light between shafts, white walls to bounce it up, and a frosted shell for diffusion. The printer did three filament swaps per layer, leaving a mountain of purge waste. I put a 256-pixel matrix inside and turned it on. Heat built up fast. I picked the piece up after a burn-in test and accidentally mushed the softened grid in with my thumb.

Venting the back helped, but drilling holes in the front would ruin the look. I swapped to 12-volt matrices, kept the diodes a centimeter off the surface, and set a 1-amp current limit in the software. The piece hung at Glow Lounge in Denver and ran for months without warping, proving out a single-piece fabrication rule I still use.

title: Mini Pyramid
description: An 8x8 pixel matrix desk lamp powered over 5V USB-C with a scannable QR code base.
longDescription:
Stepping down from my 16x16 matrix to an 8x8 desk piece meant solving a packaging problem. I modeled the Pixel Mini Pyramid in SolidWorks and Blender around an ESP32 running WLED on 5V USB-C power. The base doubles as a scannable QR code that links to my site.

Squeezing 64 LEDs into the small footprint left very little room for hardware. The USB-C port wanted to push back into the case whenever I plugged a cable in, and closing the shell kept crushing the internal wiring. It took several 3D printed iterations and test fits to anchor the controller securely and route the leads cleanly.

A short throw distance usually creates hotspots. I used a frosted diffusion layer over white cell walls to break up the light, and printed the case in 3 materials on an X1C. A few friends and family have them on their desks now, and the QR code base still scans on the first try.

title: Plane Warp
description: Trapped heat destroyed the first print, so I lined the cells to bounce the light instead of forcing it.
longDescription:
In a dark room, the black structure of this piece disappears, leaving only a distorted grid of light floating overhead. Plane Warp is a 16x16 matrix with a sweeping surface wave that ends in sharp points.

Because the wave's peak sits far above the base, lighting the corners meant running the LEDs at full brightness. I destroyed an early print trying to push enough light up there. The trapped heat ruined it.

It hung on the ceiling at Glow Lounge for a while. To get it there, I changed the cell design. I printed black walls to isolate each channel, lined the insides with white, and added a frosted diffusion layer. That combination became the rule: bounce the light instead of forcing it. It let me cap the controller to a one-amp limit, and the plastic survived.

title: Temple SF
description: Temple Nightclub | San Francisco - Routing a three layer club rig through an inherited lighting console to survive single operator control.
longDescription:
The owners at Temple San Francisco wanted 1 person to operate the lighting, video, and pixels in the main room simultaneously. That was never going to work with 2 hands, especially since we were stuck with the Road Hog 4 that came from the last rig. It lacked the routing capability to act as a central hub. Releasing a DMX overwrite on that console took a macro requiring dozens of screen presses. That cost several seconds, which meant missing the drop on any heavy track.

I bypassed the console entirely by routing Art-Net out of Resolume and the Hog into Madrix. I merged them using highest takes priority (HTP) on the RGB channels across 8 universes of sACN. That gave instant control back and forth just by blacking out 1 system. I also routed the video so a clip on the ceiling sliced across the main screens, overrode console colors, and drove the pillar pixels. Mask patterns kept the intensity in check. Behind the booth, I built a dedicated Resolume server with RAID6 SSDs to push simultaneous 4K layers, and we installed 400 A and 200 A electrical services to power the room. My crew built wireless receivers using ESP32s for the acrylic VIP tables and I installed a pixel wall on the mezzanine for matching ambiance.

I tore the pixel mapping down to the ground 6 times before I got all 3 systems talking to each other clean. The first night they fired together without tearing, I got goosebumps. But my control scheme was too ambitious. I installed a 65 in touchscreen running OSC Pilot to handle signal routing and live previews. It technically worked, but live operation under pressure is a different beast. The operators ripped the screen out after a few months and went back to MIDI controllers.

The demand for 1 operator survived for slow nights. Using a global fader for blackouts and the video routing from the ceiling, 1 person could run the whole room from a couple of controllers. But for busy nights and headlining DJs, the reality of the rig won out. They put 2 operators in the booth.

title: Field Solder Station
description: A compact solder station built to survive ladder work and crawl spaces during a nightclub remodel.
longDescription:
The Temple SF remodel required 80 vertical pixel strips running 4m straight up from the dance floor. 8 strips covered each pillar, which meant soldering bases at ground level or working from lifts and ladders. My bench setup was useless there. I needed a compact carrier for a TS100 iron, solder spool, flux, wick, desoldering pump, sponges, and 2 helping hands.

Early prototypes used integrated rechargeable batteries. That added too much risk, so I stripped the design down to not integrate power at all. The first field version was a rough assembly held together by tape and magnets. I iterated on it over 1 year as the remodel expanded.

I modeled the final chassis in SolidWorks and printed it in PLA on Bambu Lab printers. Precision tolerances secure the hardware through a friction fit without secondary fasteners. The helping hands are stiff enough that I have to hold the base down to bend them, but it became my main iron for pixel work.

title: LED Pixel Panel
description: Temple Nightclub | San Francisco - With eight feet from tile to joists and a basement ceiling gutted to the wood, we bolted custom LED dancefloor boards directly to aluminum T-track to build an array under an inch thick.
longDescription:
We ripped out and rerouted the fire suppression system and two layers of ceiling drywall just to buy a little breathing room. From the tile floor to the bottom of the wooden joists was exactly 8 feet, and every 1/4" mattered. Half the joists up there were broken anyway, so I had those fixed and the others restructured to push electrical, data, and HVAC down the runs of the room in line with the pillars, leaving the center in between clear.

We needed a rigid, identical grid that could hold a diffuser at an even distance without sagging. Strips droop, and wiring them is a mess. Large, cheap rigid PCBs are a good solution, so we took LED dancefloor boards and had the manufacturer alter the pixel spacing, enlarge the mounting holes, and swap in 90-degree headers. We bolted them straight into aluminum T-track mounted to the ceiling infrastructure, compressing a 24-volt WS2818 pixel matrix into a vertical profile under an inch.

I never actually saw it powered on overhead. By the time the basement was ready for the hang, I had hit my breaking point with the remodel and walked away. I had completed the upstairs main room immersive dance lighting rig during the COVID-19 pandemic and had designed and procured the parts for the basement. I pixel-mapped the array flat across a sea of road cases in the unfinished basement, proved it worked, and handed the plans off to my crew to finish the hang.

title: LVL
description: Temple Nightclub | Denver - I salvaged 8 dead pixel runs from ruined floor channels and rewired them for 3D voxel mapping.
longDescription:
When I walked into LVL, the side room at Temple Denver, the lighting rig was dead or stuck on solid blue. Someone had installed unsealed channels in the floor, and the wood support strips had absorbed months of spilled drinks, mop water, and sewage backups until the diffusion caved in and shattered. Even the foam tape holding the strips smelled like club funk. The EnvironmentalLighting pixel tape itself was expensive and salvageable, so I cut out the shorted sections, scrubbed the tracks, and built new structural support out of acrylic.

Wiring 16 strip runs across a room requires heavy power injection to stop voltage drop. My first attempt was immediately unstable. I ran DC wire in parallel and tied the negative leads together back in the supply room, which wasn't sufficient and triggered ground loop flicker across part of the system. The fix was coupling the negative leads close to the pixels above the dancefloor in addition to at the power supplies. The 12V pillar modules also fought me because of undersized wire, so I added more injection points and ground jumpers between sections until the signal stabilized. The ceiling and floor ran on 24V tape and behaved once the grounds were tied overhead.

With the power and data lines stable, I mapped all 16 floor and ceiling runs plus the pillars into a 3D voxel setup. The room runs almost entirely on those pixels, so getting the hardware clean mattered. Now the control system drives spatial sweeps through the floor, pillars, and ceiling without a single drop.

title: MIRUS
description: Blasting saturated light against white walls washes out the art, but the paintings were psychedelic anyway.
longDescription:
Someone handed me a parts list and told me to build a ceiling rig. Another crew had already hung eighty wooden baffles twelve feet above the floor. I spent the project on a scissor lift, pressing RGBW wash strips into routed channels upside down. The channels had sharp ninety-degree corners. Bending flexible copper tape around those turns snapped the backing. I ended up doing quite a lot of repairs.

To keep the install clean, I ran the wiring out the ends of the wood and straight up into a six-foot plenum. I walked across the rafters up there to build the control system. I grouped the baffles into ten zones, pairing one power supply to one DMX decoder with 8 outputs. The power units they bought ran with loud fans. Usually, that ruins an art gallery. Luckily, the room shared a door with a nightclub. The ambient bass swallowed the fan hum.

I wired the decoders to control each baffle individually while keeping the ceiling on a single DMX universe. During the day, the room needed flat white illumination. At night, we flipped a preset and the ceiling ran heavy color chases. Blasting saturated light against white walls completely washed out the art. Because most of the paintings were psychedelic anyway, I threw out standard gallery rules. We let the colors bleed and turned the room into an extension of the dance floor.

title: Inflatable Tubes
description: Crawling inside an inflated three-foot cylinder on a concrete floor is a disorienting way to wire pixels.
longDescription:
The centerpiece for Denver Pride was an array of eight inflatable tubes rigged to the ceiling beams. Standard LED tape was never going to cut through a club lighting rig. I ordered custom 24-volt pixel strands with double-sided clear lenses. I inflated the three-foot tubes on the concrete floor, turned the strands on, and crawled inside to tie the wiring down. It was disorienting. The tubes had strange twists in unusual directions, and dragging myself over the concrete hurt.

I ran two strands in parallel inside each tube. Pushing that much load causes voltage drop, so I put a power supply at both ends and severed the positive wire at the midpoint to stop back-feeding. We hoisted them empty and powered the fans in the air. The wireless control system worked perfectly during load-in. Then two thousand people walked into the room. Their cell phones choked the RF environment. Data rates dropped to five frames per second, and the tubes lost connection.

I used wireless decoders to save money. It is a choice I would reverse today. Luckily, I programmed their default state to a static Pride palette. When the signal dropped, the centerpiece stayed on theme. The rig pushed out enough light that another fabricator called me later to ask what hardware I used. I got the venue through the weekend on the fallback palette and told them to hardwire the data next time.

title: GeoLens Pro
description: I built a localized browser app that automatically sorts field photos by GPS coordinate into project folders.
longDescription:
Doing custom lighting work around Denver meant taking quick reference photos on my phone all day. Every picture dumped into a single camera roll, and I never spent the time to sort them later. I also had loose wiring notes, drawings, and measurements that needed to stay with the right job.

To fix that, I built a browser app in React 18 and TypeScript that sorts incoming photos by GPS coordinate automatically. Using Leaflet for map boundaries and exifr to read file metadata, the app runs Haversine math against active project geofences. Photos taken inside a boundary drop straight into that project folder. Anything it misses lands in a bin for manual sorting.

For notes, I built a canvas editor to layer virtual transparencies over the photos. I could circle a part or scribble a measurement, then export a PDF report using jsPDF. Dexie handles the IndexedDB storage locally, while Supabase and Lovable manage the backend and deployment. I left contract work before running it through a full season, but the core engine did what I needed.

title: PixelForge
description: A web workspace that uses hallucinated text prompts to break repetitive visual loops in image generation.
longDescription:
Standard image generators get boring fast. I built PixelForge to see what happens when a language model hallucinates an abstract, poetic foundation before any rendering starts. The frontend runs on React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS. It connects the Gemini API for prompt generation to the Imagen or NanoBanana API for the final render, and stores the whole session history locally in IndexedDB and LocalStorage.

Early iterations got stuck in a visual loop. The app kept generating characters in the same poses or returning to identical themes. It was accidentally feeding pieces of previous prompts into the new input context. I spent hours going back and forth with Gemini and later Cursor to isolate the client-side state and force the app to forget old generations between runs.

Even with a clean state, individual models drift toward repetitive styles over time. I added a manual model selector in the settings menu to route prompts across different versions. That switch breaks the visual convergence by letting different models interpret the same parameters, and it keeps the app functional as older models retire.

title: Chronicle: Iterative Fiction Engine
description: I built a browser-based storytelling engine in zero-build React that generates text, illustrations, and audio entirely client-side.
longDescription:
I wanted an interactive storytelling game inspired by the retro aesthetic in Mr. Robot, and I wanted to host it for free on GitHub Pages. That meant zero backend and no bundlers. I started the prototype in a Gemini Canvas and kept the zero-build architecture when I moved the codebase over to GitHub, wiring React 18, ES modules, and Tailwind CSS directly through the browser. Every turn runs client-side and hits the Google Gemini API to build the narrative, 4 player choices, an illustration, and spoken audio.

The first attempts fell apart fast. Without a strict memory structure, image styles drifted after a few turns, the story got stuck in loops, and the narrative would ramble with no clear end. Keeping track of earlier events inside a growing prompt was the hardest part. I had to build a memory stack that compresses older beats into shorthand summaries while passing along the recent prose and visual reference tags.

Each turn triggers several API calls at once to generate the prose, questions, image, audio, and log updates. With heavier models, a single turn took upwards of 2 minutes to load. I switched to default models to drop the wait down to 15 to 20 seconds. It works well enough for my own playthroughs, but managing that much client-side state without a build step is painful enough that I plan to rebuild the entire engine from scratch.

title: Strata - Digital Notebook
description: I built a serverless digital notebook that embeds Google Drive files inside a custom client-side canvas.
longDescription:
Flipping through dozens of Google Docs, Sheets, and Slides every day at Boston Dynamics got exhausting without a clear hierarchy to organize them. I wanted a OneNote layout with notebooks, tabs, and pages, but I refused to pay for a server. Piping everything straight through the Google Drive API and browser storage solved the hosting cost, but it meant building the engine from scratch.

To embed webpages directly into notebook pages, I built a desktop prototype to dodge iframe security blocks. The desktop build worked, but needing an installed app killed the convenience of opening a workspace on any browser. I abandoned the desktop build, accepted the iframe limitations, and pivoted back to the web application.

The browser fought back on performance. Canvas zooming stuttered, and touchscreen inputs refused to line up with SVG drawings. While I sorted out the coordinate math, sync remains a headache. Edits sometimes drop, and deleted pages occasionally resurrect themselves on reload. Strata is still an active work in progress, but the client-side layout is set.

title: IdeaForge.AI
description: I built a multi-stage idea sifter that runs its entire backend on the Google Sheets and Drive APIs.
longDescription:
People like to treat early concepts like target practice. They shoot holes in an idea before it has room to breathe. I wanted a sifter that takes raw dumps of thought and builds them up without initial critique. I first prototyped the workflow in Notion and rebuilt it with Lovable and Supabase, but both meant recurring monthly subscriptions. I stripped out the cloud database entirely and wired the application directly into the Google Sheets and Google Drive APIs.

The frontend runs on React and TypeScript, with a local data layer handling offline edits and reconciliation against the spreadsheet. Users drop in raw thoughts, and a Gemini integration tags and summarizes them. When a concept shows promise, you promote it to a brainstorm. The model runs an interview to extract missing detail, then compiles an execution strategy, an expense tracker, and a structured task list.

Every user already has a Google account, so the backend infrastructure costs nothing to run. I put my custom lithophane generator, LithoLab, through the campaign pipeline to test the playbook generation. Instead of killing half-formed ideas early, the workflow pushes them into actionable phases until you can see whether they actually work.

title: CharGen.AI
description: I built a browser-based character engine that turns 100 attributes into structured profiles and Imagen 4.0 artwork.
longDescription:
I wanted to generate varied, realistic characters across human and fantasy archetypes without paying for server infrastructure or storing user data. I built the entire engine to run locally in the browser using React 18, Vite, and Zustand. The interface uses an 8 section builder with over 100 conditional attributes that adapt dynamically to species selection. Users plug in their own Google API keys, and the application coordinates Gemini 2.5 Flash for text generation and Imagen 4.0 for visual synthesis, saving complex JSON objects and image payloads directly to IndexedDB.

I started the build in Gemini Canvas, but the app rotted once the single file hit 1000 lines of code. Options disappeared, previous settings reverted, and the interface broke completely. I moved the project to Cursor and GitHub to break the architecture into modular files. Once the app compiled reliably, the AI models struggled with basic logic. Without context, the randomizer picked identical stats repeatedly. The vision pipeline also fought clothing layers. When a prompt described muscle definition, the model rendered bare skin right through the shirt. I reduced that visual bleed by looping reference images back through NanoBanana to enforce outfit consistency.

The engine now operates in 2 directions. I can generate a character from scratch and lock specific parameters like species or clothing, or I can feed reference art into the vision model to extract structured physical and psychological data. It serves as a working proof of concept, and I plan to use the underlying system to drive an AI tabletop RPG generator and a random persona chat tool.

title: LithoPalletGen
description: A zero-dependency calibration tool that averages pixel data from physical filament swatches for multi-material lithophane printing.
longDescription:
A sunflower field photo of my partner and me printed in CMYW left our faces covered in maroon splotches. Layer thickness kills light transmission before CMYW can produce realistic skin tones. I bought a 2nd AMS2 for extra filaments, but I still needed accurate calibration data.

My calibration template is a 4x5 grid of 25 mm squares scaling in 0.05 mm steps over a 0.15 mm white backing. I print the swatches at 100% infill, photograph them on a light panel, and upload the image. Even off an X1C, surface texture breaks a single-pixel eyedropper reading. I wrote an area-averaging sampler in vanilla JavaScript that aggregates up to 256 pixels to grab the true color of each thickness. Collapsible palette sets keep the interface readable across multiple materials.

Having zero dependencies lets me host the app free on GitHub Pages. The engine exports a HSL or hex JSON to import into LithoLab, my PIXEStl-based generator. Skin tones on the next print came out clean, and I dropped to a 0.2 mm nozzle to push the detail.

title: Field Bench PSU
description: A 3D printed, portable, DC power supply built from a buck-boost converter designed for testing LED lighting installations in the field.
longDescription:
On-site LED pixel work always runs on 5V, 12V, or 24V DC at under 5A. I wanted to test new strips and isolate lighting sections without dragging a heavy bench supply up a ladder. A PLA+ enclosure housed a buck-boost converter, commonly fed 19V from a 100W laptop brick through a USB-C to 5521-DC adapter cable or a 24v 5a brick. I left a direct USB-C port off the chassis because my print tolerances could not hold one cleanly.

Assembling the wiring inside the box was a challenge. I had to build an awkward ring-crimp split to feed the banana plugs, and threading the retaining nuts on in that cramped footprint was frustrating. The screw terminals on the back of the converter module also fought me as I slid the unit into the shell.

I first brought it to Que Bueno Suerte to test 5m blackout pixel tubes on the mezzanine, verifying every strip before and after cutting. It survived a few years of site work until the built-in voltage meter drifted out of spec and I retired it.

title: Club Lexi
description: I anchored 64 fixtures straight into the joists and locked the controller so DJs couldn't mess up the presets.
longDescription:
Club Lexi is a basement trapped under a ceiling just short of ten feet. If I used standard box truss, patrons would be hitting their heads on the moving lights. I hung the entire lighting system from strut channel anchored straight through the drywall into the joists. Working flush against a ceiling leaves zero room to hide a mess. Everything is exposed. I laid out the fixtures in straight lines so I could bundle the cables into tight runs.

An electrician dropped power on dedicated switches, letting the venue kill half the rig early in the night without touching the software. I packed 64 fixtures into the space. I programmed the presets alone on the dance floor with the music blasting. Putting moving heads right above people means watching every inch of clearance. My rule was to never have all fixture types on at the same time. Firing everything at once in a room that low was blinding and unpleasant.

The venue operates without a technician, so a Wolfmix controller sat in the booth for the DJs. Handing them live control immediately exposed the weak points. They dragged fade times to a crawl and assumed the rig was broken when the lights stopped moving. They also mashed the strobe button until the room was unreadable. I locked the hazer to a low-output toggle, built pre-programmed looks to enforce my lighting rules, and set up a hard reset so they could not trap the program.

title: The Orb
description: Temple Nightclub | Denver - I finished an 8 ft aluminum LED sphere and ran high-current DC power over 35 ft.
longDescription:
The original installer walked away mid-job, leaving an 8 ft aluminum sphere sitting in 2 halves on the top-floor. 1 dome was partly covered in LED pixel modules zip-tied to the metal, with tape over the lenses and black spray paint over the rest. Masked strands lay scattered across the floor. I stripped the mess and started over.

Keeping the power supplies in the ceiling left empty space inside the frame for the 3D effect, but it meant pushing DC power across a 35 ft run. To beat the voltage drop, I installed MEAN WELL supplies with load sharing and remote sense that adjusted output voltage in real time. Every circuit stayed under 80% capacity at 100% white load. Inside the sphere, decoders handled the signal for a 3D voxel map in Madrix.

The whole rig hung from a hoist that dropped it over the crowd. Moving heavy copper without snagging required a PVC pipe with a flange mounted through the center of the orb. I spiral-wrapped 2/0 welding cables around each other and fed them down through the pipe. That guide kept the cables clean during motion and stopped the sphere from spinning as it traveled.

We finished the build for New Year's Eve 2018. People on the dance floor mostly miss it, but the surrounding VIP tiers get a clear view of the full voxel map. Every night around midnight, the hoist dropped the sphere with the headliner.

title: The Basement
description: I hid hundreds of pixels on top of wooden slats and bounced the wash off the bare concrete.
longDescription:
The basement at Triangle had a concrete ceiling at 10ft high. I despise looking directly at bare light sources. Instead of covering an overhead array in standard diffusion, I decided to bounce the light. A carpenter hung 62 slats under the concrete, leaving a four-inch gap. I mounted a 20-pixel strand on top of each slat, pointing straight up.

I prepped the strands on the ground and wired them as the carpenter worked. I also hung moving lights in the remaining space. That meant rotary-hammering strut channel directly into the ceiling. You get really good at working one-handed when you have to balance on a ladder, hold a fifteen-pound fixture, and thread a bolt. During testing, a loose connection caused the ground to drop and the pixels to flicker. I had zip-tied the wiring tight. With only four inches of clearance, I couldn't squeeze my hands in to pull the cables down. I had to pry the slats back off the ceiling to fix the joints.

I isolated the power supplies in an adjacent room. I didn't know fanless supplies existed then, but the quiet room made programming easier. When the rig ran, you never saw a source. The reflected wash bled through the gaps and filled the negative space. It took fluid and fire effects perfectly, and hiding the hardware kept a low room from feeling crowded.

title: Que Bueno Suerte!
description: Que Bueno Suerte! | Denver - Over 2 years, I wired 11 custom lighting installations into a single restaurant server rack.
longDescription:
My friend let me perpetually add lighting inside Que Bueno Suerte! over 2 years, eventually totaling 11 distinct installations. With so many LEDs, the system risked overpowering the dining room. Finesse was key. Deep reds, oranges, and yellows looked phenomenal against the gold walls and red accents, but only if the hardware stayed invisible in broad daylight. I ran long-range decoders back to a server rack in the upstairs office. Wires snaked under bars, behind walls, above the kitchen ceiling, and inside rafters upstairs. Retrofitting the acrylic etchings meant climbing over tables while brittle adhesive exploded into fine powder that turned sticky again the second I sweated.

I built an iPad remote early on using OSCpilot for touch control and Show Cockpit for signal distribution. Originally, I ran ELM on the server because it was cheaper and isolated the different rigs easily. The tradeoff was programming flexibility. I couldn't transition one element at a time without shifting the entire building. Switching to Madrix solved the visual output, creating room looks that shifted together across the mezzanine ceiling, alabaster bartop, bottle shelves, and roof liners.

A rig of this complexity in a packed restaurant breaks in predictable ways. The PixLite 16 controllers above the main bar occasionally drop data and require a breaker flip to reboot. The wireless etchings lose signal through dense crowds. Outdoor fixtures leak water, break their IP rating, and trip breakers. Even the iPad control drops out if staff connect to the wrong network or the WLAN hiccups.

To keep the system usable for bartenders during a rush, I locked the iPad interface down to basic parameters and playlists of preset looks. For everything else, I installed a slide-out KVM in the rack so I could fix server issues directly. The fine control over the building proved worth the routing headaches, and the warm palettes still sit right in the room.

title: Bar Tubes
description: Que Bueno Suerte! | Denver - Rebuilding an inherited array of 131 recycled fluorescent tube bundles over an operating bar required 70 universes of control and a 3D voxel map.
longDescription:
The vertical tubes above the main bar at Que Bueno Suerte! came with the building, and by the time I got to them, they needed serious help. The array was made of 62 four-foot and 69 eight-foot recycled fluorescent tubes hung in clusters of 3, with 60/m density LED tape running down the center. After years above a bar, the materials were brittle, and because the restaurant was open every day, I could only take down a few clusters at a time. I stood on a telescoping ladder resting on the ceiling grid (which flexed enough to make every climb interesting), lowered the clusters onto the bar, broke the old wraps, and pulled the dead strip from the center.

I kept the original pixel spacing so I wouldn't have to redesign the physical bundle, but I swapped the strip for WS2813 LEDs. The backup data line meant a single failed pixel wouldn't force another sketchy ladder climb over an open bar. Up in the custom power boxes, I gutted the original decoders, which had zero documentation, and replaced them with Advatek PixLite 16s to tie the array into the venue-wide system I installed. When I first fired the rig up, it immediately tripped breakers and blew the inline fuses. I eventually bumped the fuse rating to 7A per tube to handle the inrush, and the rig stabilized.

Because I was locked into the original 60/m density, the display takes an astronomical 35,640 channels across 70 universes to run. Once the hardware was solid, I built a 3D voxel map of the entire layout. Because the tubes hang at uneven lengths and the display isn't a straight line, clean 3D effects can get lost if you push them too hard. But isolating different zones and mapping through the depth of the room turned a partially dead, inherited fixture into the centerpiece of the bar.

description: An internal X obstruction inside each cell turns a white square into an array of 1024 converging arrows.

I wanted to build the pixel diffusion equivalent of a stage gobo. I designed an X obstruction through the center of 256 isolated cells in SolidWorks. Powered off, the piece sat like a plain square. My first attempt on a Tenlog TL-D3 failed when the nozzle dragged across the X pattern and caused layer shifts. Printing directly against the buildplate kept the face flat. A 1 mm PLA+ face provided the right balance of diffusion and opacity without bleeding light between cells.

I capped the current in WLED on an ATHOM ESP8266 controller to stop the PLA+ from heating and warping. Running fluid patterns across the grid made the uniform obstructions look fuzzy and ripply.

title: Seed of Life
description: A 1mm face printed over a subdivided matrix hides the seed of life until the pixels fire.
longDescription:
I built this as a proof of concept to expand what I could do with subdivided matrices. Printed face down, the piece looks like a white square when turned off. Getting that surface required a 1mm face. That thickness balanced structural stability and light transmission without showing bleedthrough from the black walls behind it. With a 10mm throw, bouncing the light was unnecessary.

Heat became the immediate problem. Early tests ran at full brightness inside sealed enclosures. Over time, the corners curled and the grid walls softened enough to move by hand. Without vent holes on the back, the units bowed away from the wall as the PLA+ heated up. Adding vents and limiting current in the firmware stopped the deformation.

Now the symbol stays hidden until the matrix powers on. Lighting large clusters of pixels reveals parts of the pattern across the surface. The complete shape only appears when every pixel is active.

description: I embedded a 256-pixel matrix inside a relief carving, printing double black walls to stop the light bleed.

I wanted to map a rigid geometric matrix inside an organic shape. This piece is a dual-material relief sculpture of a Celtic owl. When powered off, the front face acts like a lithophane, reading as a white carving in a black frame. Turn it on, and a 16x16 LED grid cuts straight through the surface lines.

My workstation laptop crashes if I calculate an internal grid larger than 16x16. I bought an owl model online and split the workflow between SolidWorks and Blender. Subtracting those 256 cells from the knotwork pushed the hardware to its limit.

Early prints leaked light everywhere. Stopping the bleed initially took 0.8 mm walls, requiring two passes with the nozzle. Moving the job to a Bambu Lab X1C with an AMS unit solved it. The fabrication rule became simple: a double 0.4 mm wall of black PLA+ now isolates every cell cleanly.

title: Lobby Wall
description: Tracks | Denver - I built a double-sided wall of LEDs for Tracks in 5 days after soldering 5000 joints by hand.
longDescription:
Tracks could not close for a remodel, so we had 5 days between open weekends to install a double-sided wall of LEDs and as part of a full remodel. It sits right at the entrance where people walk in. To hit that window, another tech and I spent weeks in the club basement and my home shop building modular panels off site. Each 2x4 pegboard panel held 520 raw LED pucks contact-cemented in 8 pixel configurations. Instead of buying pre-made strands, we manually soldered custom wire lengths using lamp cord for power injection, leaving us with over 5000 solder points before we ever hung a panel.

We mounted the rows of pegboard modules to the wall and wired each row to a dedicated output on a 16 output SanDevices E682 decoder running WS2801 protocol. Frosted plexiglass sheets on standoffs covered both sides to diffuse the light. I mapped the array using Madrix 3.6 software.

This was one of my first LED pixel builds, and the initial test run was rough. The pixels flickered badly across the wall. I had not linked grounds across multiple power supplies, and I did not know about power injection yet. Adding inline resistors at the inputs smoothed out the data signal, and I later retrofitted power injection at the midpoint. The E682 is a Christmas light decoder and not very rugged, but it worked.

When we opened the doors that Thursday, regulars gasped walking into the room. Teaching myself pixel mapping on that build launched an entire lighting design focus in my career, even if I should have just bought pre-made LED strands.

title: Curved Liquor Bottle Display
description: I printed 96 louvered tracks with tolerances so tight a solder joint would prevent assembly.
longDescription:
I refused to put a diffuser over the LEDs and kill the brightness. The liquor display was an open metal grid. I wanted to hit the glass bottles from multiple angles to make them pop. To preserve the throw distance while hiding raw diodes from guests, I needed custom louvered fixtures.

I designed the tracks and ran my 3D printers for a couple of weeks to manufacture 96 units. A flat bracer slid in behind the LED strip to hold it against the plastic. The fit was so tight I had to use un-spliced sections, because a solder joint would not clear the gap. The diodes poked perfectly through the slots. I wired them all at my house, hiding a strain relief inside the end caps.

The metal frame started at hip level. I sat on a checkout table behind it and used foam tape to mount the fixtures into the corners. With nowhere to hide wiring, I wrapped the routing in black tubing and let the stiff bundle support itself across the gaps.

The array tied into the building's Madrix server. It worked cleanly until guests started abandoning drinks on the shelf. Spills dripped down and corroded the unsealed tape. Because my printed tolerances were so tight, waterproof tape would not fit as a replacement. I had to pry five fixtures off the metal and completely rebuild them. I asked management for a sign to not put drinks there.

title: Temple Denver
description: Temple - Main Room | Denver - Bridging Resolume and Madrix over NDI to stretch a 196 pixel canvas across an entire nightclub room.
longDescription:
Touring DJs kept coming through with custom VJ content and nowhere to realistically play it. The venue had 3 screens with a 48x48 resolution, giving the main room an accumulative resolution smaller than a phone icon. To give those artists a usable canvas, I needed to span the room without tearing out the existing hardware.

This was my first time integrating systems past DMX and MIDI cross triggers alone. Resolume Arena pushed slices of video to converter boxes that output SPI pixel signals, while Madrix ran the floor-to-ceiling custom pixel pillars with about 12 modules per row. Bridging the two over NDI let the content cross between machines. From there, I added DMX triggers from our Roadhog 4 console to the main pixel and video rigs, plus the orb and hallway computers, so we could grab master intensity and speed live.

Getting the low resolution pixel mesh to map onto the frosted pillars was the hardest problem to solve. The pixel spacing was not an even grid, which made scaling irregular shapes across the room a constant headache. If I were building the rig from the ground up, I would have chosen Madrix for the entire system.

Combining the setups got us an uninterrupted canvas just under 200 pixels wide. A couple of friends were working with me at the time, and we all geeked out when it finally came together. We could display logos and short messages across the whole wall.

title: Extrusion Centering Sled
description: A 4 part 3D printed sled aligned 160m of vertical LED track across 10 wavy nightclub pillars.
longDescription:
Temple nightclub in San Francisco had 10 foundational pillars going from floor to ceiling. Each 4m column was boxed in and wavy, but needed 12mm LED track centered vertically on all 4 sides. Because the thin lines mirrored across the room, any drift would be obvious.

Standard measuring was useless on the uneven casing. I built a 4 part sled that rode inside the center track, breaking the jig into pieces to beat my 3D printer build plate limit. Notched ends marked with yellow china marker referenced the outer corner extrusions at any height. My first prints did not fit inside the channel, taking a couple of tries to dial in the sled width. Once the sizing was right, the interlocking joints held rigid.

Using the tool on site was fast. As I slid the jig upward, it actively found true center while I tacked the extrusion progressively with a pneumatic nailer. I finished all 160m of track in a couple of hours. The installation hid the wavy casing and kept every line straight.

title: Dance Floor Pillars
description: Temple Nightclub | San Francisco - I built 320 meters of custom recessed pixel tape into 10 floor-to-ceiling structural pillars on a skeleton budget.
longDescription:
We remodeled the main room at Temple Nightclub in San Francisco during the pandemic lockdowns with a skeleton crew and no budget. I was putting 320 meters of SM16704 RGBW (6000k) pixel tape seemingly built directly into 10 structural pillars on the dance floor. To build recessed tracks without expensive hardware, I wrapped the columns in OSB and mounted mud-in aluminum extrusions with a pneumatic nailer. I filled the remaining gaps with more board, plastered everything with drywall mud, and spent weeks on a scissor lift with an orbital sander hooked to a shop vac. Then I primed the columns, painted them flat black, and sealed the bottoms with silicone caulk.

The wiring had to survive crowd contact below and attic heat above. At the bottom of each column, thin metal tubing protected 3-conductor 18 AWG wiring from kick damage. Power injection runs went up inside the corner moldings to fight voltage drop across the 4 m strips. At the top, the lines met at a 24-pin ATX power coupler that connected to custom distribution boards above the video ceiling. Working up there meant crawling across strut channel and the backs of video panels in a 16 in gap, fighting condensation and heat while carpet blower fans pushed air toward the rear wall.

Just 2 weeks before we opened, the owner decided to flip the building entrance 180 degrees, but the main room layout held. Firing all 10 pillars from the dance floor looked like light jumping out of the concrete and vanishing into the ceiling above. Building custom distribution boards for morning hardware swaps took extra time that I would handle differently today, but the rig survived the crowds exactly as built.

title: Pixel Louver Lights
description: 96 3D-printed louver fixtures that illuminate 48 bar cubbies without shining raw RGB pixels at patrons.
longDescription:
The bar display at Que Bueno Suerte! has 48 cubbies arranged in 4 sets of 3x4. I needed a way to light the bottles from the front corners without blinding patrons walking past the shelves. Using Solidworks, I modeled louver fixtures and printed 96 of them across a Bambu labs X1C and a P1P. Each unit houses 12 WS2815 RGB pixels and mounts to the metal shelf with double-sided tape for simple servicing.

Getting the slide-in backing to fit required several revisions. Solder splices along the LED tape cause height variations that block the backing from sliding into place, so I cut the tape to avoid the splices entirely. I also added zip ties to hold the wiring. They act as strain relief so hanging cables never rip the solder pads off the strips.

Because the bottles sit on dry shelves, I installed non-waterproof strips. That caused problems later on. During dancing nights, patrons set drinks on the cubbies, and spills corroded and shorted the pixel strips inside the fixtures. Even with a redundant data line, a fried strip stops working, so I had to pull the dead units and replace the tape.

Running the strips into the shelves creates a 3D voxel display that sweeps light across the glass from every angle. This was the first time I designed and manufactured a 3D-printed pixel fixture for a live rig.

title: Blackout Ceiling Tubes
description: I shot a laser level under a low duct and hung a flat array that vanishes into the dark paint.
longDescription:
A central HVAC duct and a low mezzanine ceiling had already killed a previous lighting concept. I took the lowest point of that duct as a hard clearance limit and shot a laser level across the room. We hung a flat array of blackout pixel tubes. Standard milky white LED diffusion looks cheap when powered off. I used black diffusion against dark ceiling paint so the rig would visually disappear during the day.

We assembled the five-meter tubes on the floor. A friend helped me lift them onto two six-foot ladders, stringing them up and leveling them a few inches at a time. I originally ran wire inside the casing for power injection at the far end, but it drooped and cast shadows. I ripped the extra wiring out. The strips ran full white from a single end with zero color shift. Black diffusion eats light, but pixel rigs are usually too bright anyway. The physical dimming was exactly what we wanted.

Silent operation meant no fanned power supplies. I split eighteen waterproof units across three circuits. Booting them at once tripped the breakers instantly from inrush current. I wired generic relay PCBs into custom sequencer boxes to stagger the startup by five seconds. The hardware vanishes into the ceiling by afternoon, washes the tables in warm white for dinner, and runs heavy chases when the dance floor opens.

title: LED PSU Boot Sequencer
description: I built 3 3D-printed boot sequencers to stagger 18 power supplies without popping the venue breakers.
longDescription:
Que Bueno Suerte! needed 18 MEAN WELL HLG-320H-12 power supplies to drive an LED pixel ceiling across 3 circuits. Firing up that many capacitors at once meant tripping the breakers from high inrush current. Pulling more electrical circuits cost too much, and commercial gear was overpriced. I built 3 3D-printed boot sequencers instead, putting 6 supplies on each box.

Inside each unit, a small MEAN WELL supply ran a relay board that acted as an automated switch bank. Packing high-voltage lines, relay boards, and a nest of WAGOs cleanly into a sealed case without risking a short took several enclosure revisions. Every connection used locking connectors, with indicator LEDs on the front to show live outputs and status lights on the back to verify AC power. I capped the lighting load at 80% of maximum capacity when every channel ran at full brightness. That headroom kept heat down and made the hardware impossible to kill with software mistakes.

I mounted the boxes on the black wall just above the display rafters. Flipping the power starts a cascade of relay clicks across the room. Every 5 to 10 seconds, another ceiling section wakes up segment by segment as the capacitors charge and the DC output stabilizes. Once the boot sequence finishes, the whole rig runs silent.

title: WiFi VIP Tables
description: I salvaged 32 waterlogged acrylic VIP tables into wireless ArtNet pixel fixtures using routers and kitchen soup containers.
longDescription:
Temple SF had 32 old VIP tables with heavy laminated MDF bases and black acrylic tops. The MDF had soaked up spilled drinks for years, expanding and separating, while the acrylic had sharp, chipped corners that were a hazard in a drunk crowd. Most of the hardwired RGB wash strips underneath were already dead. Buying new plastic during the pandemic was too expensive and too slow, but the acrylic sheets were still good. I decided to strip them down and rebuild them from scratch.

My carpenter and I used a router with a shop vac attached to carve the existing acrylic channels deeper for new LED strips and cut a center path for the wiring. We rounded the top and bottom edges across all 32 sheets, which eliminated the sharp corners and gave the acrylic a smooth, clean line from every angle. To replace the ruined MDF bases, I cut plywood sheets, painted them black, and secured them to the underside so we could attach modern metal legs.

Time got tight toward the end, and my 3D printer could not produce clean enclosures fast enough. I walked into the kitchen, grabbed a stack of plastic soup containers, and siliconed them to the center underside of each table to house an ESP32 decoder and a Li-ion battery. The electronics sat safely out of reach of nightly spills. For power management, I built a charging station on the side of the control rack. The lighting operator gathered the batteries at the end of the night to charge them, then swapped them back in before doors opened.

I mapped all 32 tables into Madrix 5.x over wireless ArtNet so they matched the colors of the main room lighting rig. Running Wi-Fi control through a crowded club floor is always a fight against RF noise, but high-gain antennas on the receivers kept the signal alive. The tables fit the room, survived the crowd, and salvaged the most expensive material we had.

title: Glass VIP Wall
description: Temple Nightclub | San Francisco - I found thousands of dollars of buried 24V LED strip under a staircase during lockdown and turned it into a 1:1 pixel grid for the mezzanine.
longDescription:
During the COVID-19 lockdown at Temple SF, we had time on our hands and scoured the building. Back in an overflowing hallway, inside a cubby under some stairs, I found several boxes of brand new, 20m long, 24V waterproof LED strips from Environmental Lighting left over from the original install. I also found the rigid mounting track. It was thousands of dollars of high-end product buried in the bowels of the club, meant to replace a single dead strand of pixels at the bottom of the long glass mezzanine wall. I gathered enough salvaged Madrix Nebula decoders and power supplies to build a proper installation.

The glass panels were around 100 pounds each. I bought industrial suction cups, used body mechanics to get them over the lip, and walked them out by the corners to expose a five-inch working gap. I shot a laser level across the far wall to set the rigid track, then calculated the physical length of a single pixel on the strips. I set the vertical spacing between the tracks to match that measurement exactly, building a 1:1 pixel grid that ran in one continuous shot across the raised VIP area.

Even with 24V strips and thick power rails, voltage drop over a 20m run is inevitable. When I ran all channels at full white, the strips gradually tinted red toward the far end. I countered this by running an 18AWG power injection wire across the top of the channels to the opposite end, and tied the DC- lines together across the silent, waterproof power supplies and two Nebulas behind the far glass panel.

When we powered it up, the wall mapped cleanly into the main room programming and transformed the mezzanine. But it immediately created an operational problem: because the venue never fixed the house lighting in that area, our pixel wall was the primary light source for VIP. When the main dancefloor system hit a master blackout, the lounge plunged into pitch black, generating immediate complaints from people trying to drink. We ended up having to isolate the mezzanine wall to ignore master blackouts entirely.

title: Pixel Rocks
description: The director wanted hand-held props that looked sharp enough to stone someone, but glowed from the inside.
longDescription:
A lighting designer friend needed internally lit rocks for a contemporary ballet. The artistic director wanted them sharp and jagged. They had to look like they could stone someone to death, but fit in one hand.

I hiked outside Denver and collected stones that fit the aesthetic and my 3D scanner. Scanning them let me scale the models up to the size of about a pineapple. I modeled a universal sled that locked into the base of any rock. A custom puck slid inside, holding the battery, the decoder, and the pixel tape. During the run, the live network choked the 2.4GHz decoders, causing some units to freeze on stage. I never used 2.4GHz for show control again.

The design worked because of one fabrication rule: absolute modularity. I printed the clear PLA shells at five percent infill to keep the brightness high, and built the internal hardware to slide out with a single threaded cap.

title: Backboard
description: Temple Nightclub | Denver - I rebuilt a failing 36x40 resolution LED backwall at Temple Denver to eliminate an active fire hazard.
longDescription:
Temple Denver brought me in to fix a swept LED backwall on their main stage. I pushed 100% intensity through all channels to see where the rig stood. The 36x40 resolution wall was a fire hazard. The previous installer misunderstood load calculations and wire gauges. Severed cables were shorting against the metal frame and melting.

Getting to the hardware proved worse than the electrical work. The wall curved into a sloped ceiling directly above the DJ booth and VIP seating. I spent 3 days perched 20 ft up an extension ladder footed on a concrete access ramp. Leaning backward against the curve, I pulled and wired 30 lb plywood panels. Each 3/8 in board measured 2x4 ft and carried 20 pixel modules. We pinched a wire replacing one of them and had to drop it again for an extra repair. The wood shifts and chips every time it comes down, so I minimized removals.

I ripped out the bad distribution and installed fused DC power protection. Fresh 18awg wire went to the injection points to bypass the melted lines. I mapped the data runs and swapped the dead modules. To prevent future software-driven failures, I calculated the new hardware so a 100% software output would draw a maximum 80% physical load. The wall powered up and ran, but the existing pixel wiring was thin and brittle. Ripping the entire system out would have doubled the timeline and cost. We salvaged the existing rig, and the damage cemented my rule to mandate DC power protection on all future builds.

title: Entrance Hall
description: Temple Nightclub | Denver - I gutted and rebuilt a failing 30 ft LED entrance tunnel down to raw pixel strips to fix a rushed installation.
longDescription:
The entrance tunnel at Temple Denver was a rush job that slowly died. It was 30 ft long and never meant to be serviced. The walls were framed with 3/4 in MDF panels, which are incredibly heavy, and wires were woven haphazardly through sheet metal cutouts. Patching a failing custom LED installation is a waste of time. I decided to gut the entire run down to the pixel strips.

Mid-week gave me a 2 day window while the club was closed. Getting the tunnel open was a giant pain. I found hidden shims and adhesives in unexpected places. Pulling the aluminum extrusions was my first plan, but construction adhesive held them fast. I left the tracks in place. Removing the old soldering left me with clean copper to wire fresh. Rebuilding the power distribution from the ground up, I balanced the load across a couple 24V power supplies above the ceiling. I tied the DC- lines together to keep the data stable. Reassembling the heavy MDF meant driving screws into panels that were originally held together by double-sided tape.

My eye instantly snaps to any pixel that drops a color or gets stuck. I can spot a dead point in a data chain by instinct. Powering up the rebuilt rig lit the entire 30 ft run perfectly. Seeing a complex pixel setup firing at 100 percent is always deeply satisfying.

title: Discobasket
description: I armored LED strips for a repurposed dance platform with aluminum, heat shrink, and hot glue to survive a rowdy nightclub crowd.
longDescription:
The Tracks remodel required lighting an old dance platform that sat right in the middle of a rowdy crowd. I had to armor the rig so people could grab the cage without destroying pixels or slicing their hands. I heatshrunk LED strips to 10 mm aluminum sticks, securing them to the spokes with hose clamps buried in hot glue.

I built the 4 ft tall metal basket in half to fit it through the warehouse garage doors across the alley. I programmed the pixel map while it sat in pieces. The armored sticks survived the floor, but the sharp square channel base eventually chewed through wire insulation. Pull force ripped the solder pads, taking out 1 or 2 strips at a time until I spliced new ones in.

Data hit a decoder under the deck via a cheap AP bridge or a hardline cable. When it ran, about 6 people packed inside the cage dancing surrounded by light.

title: Pyramid Steps
description: Fixing the voltage drop meant sitting on a twelve-foot ledge over the tile with a battery-powered soldering iron.
longDescription:
The decorative pyramid above the kitchen sat twelve feet over the dining room tile. I wanted to wash the steps with pixel tape. Guests taking the stairs to the second floor had a clear view down the side. I refused to let the hardware show during the day, but it needed enough throw for a clean wash. I mounted 45-degree aluminum extrusions under the lip of each step. To make the track disappear, I pulled a paint match with a digital sensor, printed custom jigs, and sprayed the metal in batches.

The layout wrapped two sides of the pyramid. I tucked fanless power supplies in the corner, wired to receivers on the main rack. Firing it up revealed a voltage drop. The bottom steps shifted color. Fixing it meant hardwiring the corners and adding power injection at the far ends. I sat on the twelve-foot edge, splicing wire over the tile floor with a battery-powered iron. I bundled the new lines in black wire wrap, leaving a clean arc at every corner.

The painted track vanished during the day. At night, the steady voltage let the server push smooth, flowing shapes across the steps. The top of the kitchen rolled with slow waves, and on certain patterns, the pyramid looked like it was on fire.

title: Tracks Discotheque
description: I surrounded the crowd with twenty-six vintage scanners and cannibalized dead units in the basement to keep them alive.
longDescription:
Tracks was one of the last classic discotheques left in the country. The design rule was simple: surround the crowd, and keep the focus off the DJ booth. To put the audience directly inside the show, I stacked 26 vintage scanners across three layers in the ceiling. Twelve Trackspot 1s circled the dance floor. Eight Trackspot 2s flanked the sides in straight lines, and six Martin MX10s hung in tilted triangles overhead. I mixed them with pinspots, mirror balls, DataFlash strobes, and modern LEDs, all run from an old GrandMA Light Gen 1 console. Its motorized faders and audio BPM detection were exactly what the room needed.

For an unconventional layer, I built a dynamic truss warmer. I took leftover raw pixel PCBs from the Lobby Wall install, stuck adhesive zip-tie mounts to the back, and strapped them to the bottom pipe of the triangular truss. I aimed them straight up. The point was to illuminate the metal, not light the crowd. If I pointed them down, the bare diodes would sit directly in the patrons' line of sight.

The contrast between the hardware defined the look. Modern moving heads provided the brightness, but the 90s/2000's scanners were incredibly fast and locked onto a beat. The problem was keeping them alive. Stepper motor brakes failed. Scanners would start stuttering during slow movements and lose their tracking. The circuit boards were at least a decade obsolete, so we cannibalized dead units in the basement shop, replacing blown capacitors and motor drive chips to keep the rig running.

I expect a programmed sequence to look the same every time I recall it. With vintage mechanics, that was a constant fight. When a scanner lost its position mid-show, I would drop its intensity to zero and intentionally slam the mirror into its hard stops to force it back into alignment. When the room was packed and the console locked onto the beat, the sheer speed of those old scanners firing overhead proved why the classic club format worked.

title: Remote Fill Fog Jets
description: I pumped 55 gallons of fluid into the ceiling to fake a cryo blast, but the poles got slick.
longDescription:
After Denver cracked down on CO2 permits, securing clearance for an indoor cryo system became legally impossible. I adapted six Antari fog jets using fast dissipating fluid to simulate the massive cold blast the client wanted. With 16ft ceilings, staff couldn't reach them for manual refills. I set up a 55 gallon drum in the dressing room. Two ground pumps pushed fluid to two header tanks in the ceiling, feeding three jets each.

The 30 pound jets lacked a built in way to hang upside down. I built adjustable mounts using strut channel L-brackets and bolted them to the ceiling grid from a scissor lift. They required new dedicated circuits and remote booth switches. During the initial power up, one header tank started pouring fluid from the ceiling. A factory float valve was wired backward, signaling the pump to continue filling an overflowing tank. I sprinted to the dressing room to kill the power, then pulled the tank down for a replacement.

I patched the rig into their ChamSys console. The wash LEDs built into the jets colored the blast and sold the cryo illusion. It worked exactly as intended mechanically, but the vapor condensed on the stage poles. The steel became incredibly slick. The dancers commented, and the only remaining option was for the staff to wipe the poles down between sets.

title: Alabaster Bar Top
description: I had six hours each morning to lift the stone, wire new pixels, and seal it before the bartenders arrived.
longDescription:
The main bar at Que Bueno Suerte! runs the length of the dining room under vaulted ceilings. The top is solid alabaster. The original contractors wired the low-voltage LEDs using wire nuts. The connections failed, leaving dead spots across the stone. I wanted to install addressable pixels, but the venue refused to close. I had a six-hour window each morning to finish one section before the 3 PM open.

Every day, I sliced the old adhesive and lifted a piece of stone. I stripped the dead tape, installed narrow 12-volt pixels along the edges, and sealed the alabaster down with quick-dry silicone just before the bartenders arrived. The center section was worse. A 200-pound acrylic table wrapped around a support beam. I used spreader bars to lift it, unbolted the legs, and slowly inched the acrylic onto an adjacent table so it wouldn't crack. I ran new DC wire through the sheet metal studs and hid waterproof power supplies behind the kickers.

For weeks, I locked the finished sections to a static warm white to hide the construction. When the bar finally came online, my Madrix patch wasn't wide enough for a continuous 1500-pixel sweep. I stacked the strips in Z-layers and used fluid effects with mirroring to hide the seams. The alabaster was originally meant for a uniform white. Hitting it with dynamic color created deep internal gradients across the stone.

title: Bar Kicker
description: I pried heavy plywood panels up with my toe to wire custom neon flex in a two-inch gap.
longDescription:
The original lighting behind the bar was wired like a house. Someone laid a row of white LED modules flat on the floor, hoping the light would bounce through thick amber acrylic. There were nine of these kicker panels at Que Bueno Suerte, built from plywood and weighing 25 pounds each.

I pulled them down, repaired the damaged wood, and built custom neon flex using square tube and WS2814 pixels. I siliconed the flex along the waveform cuts on the back of the acrylic and taped it until it cured.

Because I was also lighting the alabaster bar top above, I had to keep pulling the kickers back off. Getting them back in was a physical fight. I had two inches of clearance blocked by a steel rail. I wedged my heel on the rail, pried a 25-pound sheet up with my toe, and disconnected leads blind with my free hand. I dropped two panels doing this. The impact ripped the silicone right off the back. I remounted the flex with industrial tape on the fly.

When I finally powered the rig up, the physical materials dictated the programming. The amber acrylic completely ate the blue spectrum. I dropped blue from the palette entirely. I built a series of slow sweeps using only red, green, and warm white, giving the lower bar a heavy, saturated accent.

title: Bar Backsplash
description: I anchored a ratchet strap to a patio fence and spent four hours hammering a trapped LED track sideways.
longDescription:
The bar backsplash was a massive acrylic wall extending to a vaulted ceiling. The original LEDs were dead. I needed to relight the acrylic edges and underlight three glass shelves. The wall was never meant to come apart. The shelves were mounted directly through the acrylic, trapping the bottom LED track under the panels. It was also locked down with double-sided tape. The top and side strips came out quickly. The bottom track was an eight-foot problem.

My only option was pulling it sideways. I drilled a hole through the aluminum track, hooked a ratchet strap to it, ran the strap out the door, and anchored it to a metal patio fence. I slid a piece of strut channel through the strap as a strike plate. I stood next to the bar and hit the strut with a deadblow. The track inched out fraction by fraction. It took four hours of hammering to clear the wall.

Assembly went faster. I skipped the adhesive and slid the new track into the gap. For the shelves, I mounted pixel tape into black channels, firing light up through the bottles. Because the shelves were bolted through the wall, I could not hide the cables. I put the wires inside black wrap and pulled them perfectly straight. If wiring sits in direct eyesight, it has to look intentional. The bright acrylic acts as a backdrop for the bartenders, tying the room together.

title: Glow Lounge
description: I tucked salvaged fixtures between fixed memorial art panels and bounced tight beams off a mirrored torso.
longDescription:
The ceiling at Glow Lounge was 8 feet high. Three art panels hung over the dance floor. A community member painted them with UV paint before he passed away, so they stayed put. I scrapped my plan for pixel strips to save money and pulled down the old rig. The fixtures were gross. Dust choked the fans until they stopped spinning, causing the lights to overheat and thermal cycle. I scrubbed the salvageable units and mapped a new layout around the art.

Every inch mattered. I mounted strut channels flush to the drywall and bolted them into the joists. I tucked short beam fixtures between the panels and pushed the taller lights to the edges. I bundled the cables along the channel and balanced the rig on 2 circuits. I hung new wash lights next to the DJ, but they got stuck while panning. The metal frames bent during transport and rubbed against the housing. I just bent the yokes back by hand.

A spinning torso covered in mirrors hung over the floor. I built the show on a Wolfmix WMX1 controller. I could narrow the wash fixtures into tight beams and aim them at the torso and the mirror balls. The light shot across the room just above the crowd. If a patron was exceptionally tall, they would likely get hit in the face. The scattered reflection filled the room. It felt compact and balanced.

title: Mezzanine Bar
description: I hid twenty-three pixel segments across staggered sheet metal shelves to wash the bottles without exposing the wiring.
longDescription:
I didn't realize how the mezzanine bar at Que Bueno Suerte was built until I got there. The bottle shelves were blocks of wood with sheet metal stacked on top. I needed to wash the bottles from the front without exposing the wiring. I pre-cut 23 segments of aluminum extrusion and built the strips on a workbench. I soldered and heat-shrunk 3000K RGBW tape inside 45-degree channels, leaving wire whips on both ends.

I stuck the tracks to the top of each metal plate with foam tape. I used Dolphin crimps to splice the segments into four rows. To hide the connections, I ran cables between the wood blocks and sleeved the gaps in wire wrap.

The space under the bar had a different constraint. At night, the staff turned the mezzanine into a dance floor and shoved heavy tables underneath. Knees, coats, and sliding furniture were going to hit the lighting. I loaded more tape into an extrusion and siliconed it directly to the underside of the bar. I mounted it far enough back to survive the room flips.

Every line ran to an Advatek decoder and a power supply hidden behind the bar. I patched the rig in Madrix. Because the shelves were staggered, I had to approximate the empty space in the software patch so effects would travel at the right speed. When the rig fired up, the fire presets moved naturally across the metal plates.

title: Bubblescape
description: I fused spheres together to print a mask where no internal overhang could create a dark pocket.
longDescription:
I wanted to see a cluster of overlapping, organic shapes lit from behind. Bubblescape is a 3D-printed light piece built over a 16 x 16 pixel LED pixel matrix. Before this, I generated my internal structures in SolidWorks. But these shapes were too organic, which forced me to bring Blender into my workflow. I just took spheres of different sizes and fused them together.

The print used three materials: black for the mask, white to bounce light, and clear for diffusion. The internal geometry was a step up in complexity. The rule for these is maintaining an even internal grid. You can't let the pixels get close enough to the face to cause a hotspot. I also had to make sure there were no overhangs in the model. Any overhang creates a dark pocket that the matrix underneath can never reach.

title: Clay Face
description: I scanned my first clay sculpture and forced the rough shell to map to a rigid pixel grid.
longDescription:
I wanted to capture something rough and abstract. Clay Face is a 3D-printed LED matrix based on my first attempt at hand-sculpting. I shaped the original mask out of white modeling clay, keeping the geometry basic enough to eventually hold an internal grid.

Then I scanned it with a RevoPop hand scanner. The scan refused to cooperate. I kept getting holes in the mesh that I struggled to fill, and the model lacked the vertical height at the base to fit the hardware. I ended up doing a low-poly pass on the scan just to force a closed shape.

Once I had a solid model, I pulled it into Blender. I built out the internal subdivision to isolate the light from 256 pixels. The fabrication rule was strict: the organic, rough exterior had to map perfectly to a rigid 16 by 16 grid of black structural walls and white diffusion layers inside.

title: Scream-Face
description: I forced a flat pixel grid behind steep organic curves without letting a single diode hotspot the plastic.
longDescription:
I really liked the steep, dramatic edges of this model, but I refused to compromise the no-hotspot look. It is a 3D-printed mask illuminated by a flat 16-by-16 LED pixel matrix.

The problem with organic curves is depth. This face dips heavily into the flat surface surrounding it. When you put a rigid pixel grid behind a curved object, the distance between the light and the plastic constantly changes. The deepest parts of the mask get too close to the diodes, creating harsh bright spots.

To keep the light even, I changed how I built the internal structure. I added 10mm to the height of the grid's base layer and the outer frame. That pushed the electronics just far enough back. It all relies on a hard fabrication rule: an LED can never get closer than 10mm to the surface of the print.

title: Face
description: Making a human expression read on a low-resolution matrix meant dialing in the exact thickness of white plastic.
longDescription:
I wanted to map a human face onto a 16x16 LED matrix. It was one of the first ideas I had when I started making internally subdivided 3D prints. Face is a physical matrix that uses black plastic to mask light and white plastic to bounce and diffuse it.

I waited a few years to actually build it. My old printers could not handle the job. The surface came out too rough to read as a face, and I could not get the material thickness right. The machines also refused to print the white-lined walls I needed for internal bounce.

I shelved the idea until I had the hardware to print it properly. A newer machine solved the surface finish. I printed the mask and borders in black, and used white for the diffusion. Dialing in the exact thickness of that white layer was the rule that finally made the face readable.

title: TangiPix
description: A browser based application that reduces images into limited physical color palettes and generates printable build schematics.
longDescription:
I had several ideas for physical builds floating around in my head, like bead curtains and stacked brick images. They all required reducing a photo to a low resolution and mapping it to a strict limited color space. I built TangiPix to give myself a foundation for these projects. It operates entirely in the browser as a mosaic planner. The interface takes an uploaded photo, locks it to a physical grid, and maps those cells onto available inventory colors.

The heavy lifting happens off the main thread. I set up a Web Worker to handle the resampling and Lab color space math. Passing large pixel buffers for 15 iterations of k-means clustering would normally freeze a browser tab, so isolating that process keeps the interface responsive. I dropped G-code export from the final version because the focus remains on human assembly rather than direct machine control.

To test the engine, I ran the Mona Lisa through the pipeline and forced it into a saturated neon rainbow palette. TangiPix generated a multi page PDF schematic. The first page displayed the original photo, the converted preview, and the exact bill of materials. The rest of the document broke the grid down into numbered colored squares, ready for hand sorting.

title: BorderBuilder
description: I refuse to pay for server time when a local browser can calculate 3D geometry for custom frames.
longDescription:
I wanted nice frames for the custom lithophanes my app LithoLab generates. Initially, I planned to print the frame and lithophane as one piece. The tradeoff was time. If the frame was attached, I would have to print the whole thing with a 0.2mm nozzle. It would take forever, and the image would be permanently locked to that frame.

I split the generator into its own tool, BorderBuilder. Simple rectangles were easy. Moving to irregular shapes was a mess. Wrapping a 3D bevel around a custom mask created overlapping planes and rough edges. I debugged the geometry until the tracing worked.

A user selects their dimensions, or drops in a LithoLab export to generate a matching frame and DXF files for the acrylic panels. It runs entirely in the browser. I host it on GitHub Pages for free. I refuse to pay for server time when a local machine can do the work.
